NIGERIAN PORTS AUTHORITY

PUBLIC NOTICE ON APAPA DREDGING PLAN

The Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) wishes to inform all port users, shipping lines, terminal operators, freight forwarders, and the general public of the planned dredging of the Apapa Port channel and berth pockets. This exercise is part of the Authority’s continuing effort to maintain safe navigational depths and operational efficiency at the Lagos Port Complex.

1. SCOPE OF WORK

The planned dredging will cover the following areas:

(a) The main approach channel from the fairway buoy to the turning basin;

(b) The turning basin itself;

(c) Berth pockets along Apapa Quay, Berths 1 through 10;

(d) The area around the Apapa Bulk Terminal and the Ijora Creek entrance.

The work will involve the removal of accumulated silt and sediment to restore the designed depth of 11.5 metres below chart datum at the berths, and 13.5 metres in the approach channel. Dredged material will be disposed of at the designated offshore spoil grounds in accordance with the approved environmental management plan.

2. PLANNED DATE

The dredging is planned to commence on 2021-03-01. The Authority notes that this date is subject to weather conditions, availability of the dredging plant, and other operational factors. Any change to the planned date will be communicated through a subsequent bulletin.

3. DURATION AND WORKING HOURS

The dredging operation is expected to last approximately twenty-one (21) days, weather permitting. Works will be carried out around the clock, including public holidays, to minimise the overall duration of the exercise. The dredger and attendant tugboats will be displaying the appropriate lights and shapes at night.

4. IMPACT ON PORT OPERATIONS

During the dredging period, there will be temporary disruptions to vessel movements. These include:

(a) One-way traffic in the approach channel at certain stages of the work;

(b) Temporary closure of individual berth pockets as the dredger works along the quay;

(c) Possible delays to vessel berthing and sailing of up to four (4) hours, depending on the stage of the works.

The Authority has put in place a schedule of operations with the Harbour Master’s office to minimise these disruptions. Shipping lines and agents are advised to plan their arrivals accordingly and to liaise with the Port Master’s office for updated berthing windows.

5. SAFETY AND SECURITY

All dredging activities will be conducted in compliance with the International Safety Management (ISM) Code and the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code. The dredger will be attended by security patrol boats at all times. Unauthorised craft are warned to keep clear of the dredging area and its associated floating pipelines.

6. HEALTH, SAFETY, AND ENVIRONMENT

The contractor engaged for this exercise has been directed to comply with all applicable environmental regulations, including the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) guidelines. A pre-dredging environmental baseline survey has been completed, and water quality monitoring will be carried out throughout the operation. Any discharge of dredged material outside the approved spoil grounds is strictly prohibited.

The dredging exercise was undertaken to restore navigable depths at the port's berths, turning basin, and approach channel, which had experienced significant siltation over several years. The works were executed in accordance with the approved design depths and within the spoil grounds designated by the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA).

Key particulars of the completed works are as follows:

- Design depth at berths: 12.0 metres below chart datum
- Design depth at turning basin: 11.5 metres below chart datum
- Design depth at approach channel: 11.0 metres below chart datum
- Total volume of material dredged: approximately 1.2 million cubic metres
- Dredged material disposed at approved offshore spoil grounds

The contractor mobilised a trailing suction hopper dredger and a grab dredger for the exercise. Works commenced on 1 March 2021 and were executed in phases to minimise disruption to port operations. Berths were dredged sequentially, with each berth reopened to traffic immediately upon completion of dredging and post-dredging survey verification.

3. ACHIEVEMENTS

The completion of this dredging plan has restored the port's declared depths, thereby enabling larger vessels to berth safely and improving the overall efficiency of cargo handling operations at Apapa Port. Some of the notable achievements recorded during the exercise include:

- Restoration of full navigable depth at all six (6) berths within the port
- Reduction in vessel waiting time due to tidal restrictions
- Improved safety margins for vessels transiting the approach channel
- Compliance with all environmental monitoring requirements, with no reported incidents of unauthorised discharge

4. POST-DREDGING SURVEY

A post-dredging hydrographic survey was carried out by an independent surveyor between 10 and 14 July 2021. The survey confirmed that all dredged areas met the required design depths. The survey results have been reviewed and accepted by the Authority's Hydrographic Unit, and a copy of the survey report is available for inspection at the Port Manager's office upon written request.

5. SAFETY AND SECURITY

Throughout the dredging exercise, the Authority maintained the highest safety and security standards. The dredgers were attended by security patrol boats at all times, in compliance with the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code. No safety incidents were recorded during the period of the works.

Apapa Port actual_dredging_completion 2021-07-15 date. Record status: current.

6. HEALTH, SAFETY, AND ENVIRONMENT

The contractor complied with all applicable environmental regulations, including the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) guidelines. Water quality monitoring was carried out at specified intervals throughout the operation, and the results were within acceptable limits. All dredged material was disposed of at the approved spoil grounds, and no unauthorised discharge occurred.

7. APPRECIATION

The Authority wishes to express its sincere gratitude to all stakeholders whose cooperation and support contributed to the successful completion of this project. In particular, the Authority thanks:

- The Federal Ministry of Transportation
- The Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency (NIMASA)
- The National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA)
- The Nigeria Customs Service
- The Nigeria Police Force

- All terminal operators, shipping lines, agents, and stevedoring companies
- The contractor, Dredging International Nigeria Limited, for the professional execution of the works
- The independent surveyor, Messrs. Oceanic Surveys Limited, for the post-dredging survey

The Authority also acknowledges the patience and understanding of port users during the period of the works.

PUBLIC NOTICE ON APAPA DREDGING PLAN – SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION

Reference: NPA/LPC/PPD/VOL.3/2022/014

Date: 10 January 2022

This notice supplements the earlier Public Notice on the completion of the Apapa Port dredging works and provides information on related infrastructure projects, stakeholder engagement activities, and expected benefits. All dates and figures herein are current as of the date of this notice unless otherwise stated.

1. POST-DREDGING SURVEY AND CHART UPDATES

Following the completion of the dredging exercise on 15 July 2021, the post-dredging survey was conducted by Messrs. Oceanic Surveys Limited between 20 and 28 July 2021. The survey confirmed that the designed depths were achieved across the full width of the berthing pockets and the turning basin. The survey results have been forwarded to the Nigerian Navy Hydrographic Department for the updating of navigational charts.

Port users are advised that the electronic navigational charts for Apapa Port were updated on 12 August 2021. Mariners should ensure they are using the latest editions of all relevant charts and publications.

2. MAINTENANCE DREDGING – 2022 PROGRAMME

The Authority wishes to inform stakeholders that routine maintenance dredging at Apapa Port has been scheduled for the third quarter of 2022. This exercise will focus on the siltation hotspots identified during the post-dredging survey, particularly at the berth pockets of Berths 1 to 5 and the area adjacent to the container terminal.

The maintenance dredging programme is expected to commence in August 2022 and will last approximately six weeks, subject to weather conditions and equipment availability. The scope of works will include:

- Dredging of berth pockets to the design depth of 10.5 metres below chart datum
- Removal of accumulated silt at the turning basin edges
- Disposal of dredged material at the approved spoil grounds

The Authority will issue a separate notice with detailed information on the maintenance dredging programme, including the name of the contractor and the expected impact on port operations, in due course.

3. APAPA PORT ACCESS ROAD IMPROVEMENT PROJECT

The Authority is working with the Federal Ministry of Works and Housing and the Lagos State Government on the ongoing improvement of the Apapa Port access road network. The project, which commenced in October 2021, involves the reconstruction of the main port access road from the Apapa-Oshodi Expressway to the port gates.

As at 31 December 2021, the contractor had completed 40% of the earthworks and 25% of the drainage works. The project is scheduled for completion in June 2022. Motorists and port users are advised to expect delays and to use alternative routes where possible.

The Authority has received enquiries from stakeholders regarding the possibility of extending the scope of the road improvement project to include the rehabilitation of internal port roads. The Authority wishes to clarify that the current project scope covers only the access road outside the port gates. The rehabilitation of internal port roads is being considered under a separate project, details of which will be announced in due course.

4. STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT FORUM

The Authority held a stakeholder engagement forum on 16 December 2021 at the Lagos Port Complex Conference Room. The forum was attended by representatives of shipping lines, terminal operators, freight forwarders, customs brokers, and other port users.

The purpose of the forum was to:

- Provide updates on the completed dredging works and the post-dredging survey results
- Discuss the 2022 maintenance dredging programme
- Receive feedback from stakeholders on port operations
- Address concerns regarding access road congestion and truck turnaround times

1.0 INTRODUCTION

This report presents the consolidated performance statistics for all Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) port locations for the calendar year 2022. The data contained herein are the final year-end figures as compiled from the monthly returns submitted by the Port Managers' offices and the Harbour Masters' logs. All figures are subject to the usual verification and audit processes. This report supersedes the provisional monthly summaries issued during 2022.

2.0 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

- Total cargo throughput for all ports in 2022 was 87.4 million metric tonnes, representing a 4.2% increase over the 2021 figure of 83.9 million metric tonnes.
- Container traffic (TEU) through the Lagos Port Complex and Tin Can Island Port combined was 1.42 million TEUs, up 3.1% year-on-year.
- The average berth occupancy rate across all eastern ports was 61.3%, while the western ports recorded an average of 78.9%.
- Tin Can Island Port berth_occupancy_rate_2022 87.5 percent. Record status: current. This rate is the highest recorded among the western ports and reflects the sustained pressure on available berthing windows at that location.
- Vessel turnaround time at the Lagos ports averaged 5.2 days, a marginal improvement from 5.4 days in 2021.
- The number of vessels that called at all NPA ports in 2022 was 4,118, compared to 3,982 in 2021.

3.0 BERTH OCCUPANCY ANALYSIS

The berth occupancy rate is defined as the percentage of time that a berth is occupied by a vessel, expressed as a percentage of the total available time in the year. The figures below are calculated from the daily berth allocation logs.

Commentary:

The high occupancy rate at Tin Can Island Port is a direct consequence of the increased volume of containerised cargo, particularly from the roll-on/roll-off (RoRo) trade and the general cargo terminals. The berth occupancy rate for Tin Can Island Port is current as of the 2022 annual compilation and is reflected in the monthly dashboard maintained by the Operations Department. The port's five main berths operated at or above 80% capacity for most of the second half of the year. The situation was acute in November, when waiting time for berth allocation at Tin Can Island averaged 3.8 days for container vessels.

The decline at Calabar Port is attributed to the prolonged dredging works in the approach channel, which limited access for larger vessels. The dredging contractor reports that full channel depth will be restored by Q2 2023.

6.0 CONTAINER THROUGHPUT

6.1 Overview

Total container throughput for all Nigerian ports in 2022 stood at 1,892,400 TEU
(twenty-foot equivalent units), comprising 1,487,300 TEU of imports and 405,100 TEU of
exports. This represents an increase of 6.2% over the 2021 figure of 1,781,900 TEU.

The import/export imbalance continues to be a structural feature of the trade, with
exports accounting for only 21.4% of total containerised volume. The primary export
commodities in containers were agricultural products (cocoa, sesame seeds, cashew nuts)
and manufactured goods such as leather and textiles.

6.3 Terminal-Level Commentary

APM Terminals Apapa remains the single largest container terminal in the country,
handling 32.4% of total container throughput. The terminal operated at an average
berth productivity of 28 moves per crane-hour during the year, a marginal improvement
over the 2021 figure of 27 moves per crane-hour.

Tin Can Island Container Terminal recorded the second-highest throughput. The terminal
benefited from the diversion of some services from Apapa during the periods when the
Lagos Port Complex access road was under repair. Its average crane productivity was 24
moves per crane-hour, with a peak of 31 moves recorded in October.

Eastgate recorded a throughput of 450,000 TEU in 2022, a 7.3% increase over the
previous year. The terminal's growth was driven by the addition of two new ship-to-shore
gantry cranes in the first quarter and the expansion of its empty container storage yard,
which added 4,500 ground slots. Eastgate also reported an average truck turnaround time
of 48 minutes, which is among the best in the Western Ports complex. The terminal's
current controlled entry for 2022 is as stated above, with no pending revision.

Port & Cargo Handling Services recorded a decline of 2.6%. The decline is attributed to
the loss of one major shipping line service, which relocated to Eastgate in March 2022.
The terminal's management has indicated that it expects to recover the lost volume in
2023 through a new service agreement signed in December.

Five Star Logistics recorded the highest growth rate among the Tin Can Island terminals
at 12.4%. This growth is attributable to increased RoRo-related container movements,
as the terminal serves as a transhipment point for vehicles imported through the
neighbouring RoRo berth.

West Africa Container Terminal at Onne Port recorded the highest growth rate overall at
15.2%, albeit from a small base. The terminal is the sole container facility in the
Eastern Ports and continues to benefit from the expansion of manufacturing activity in
the Onne Oil and Gas Free Zone.

The Western Ports, comprising the Lagos Port Complex (Apapa) and Tin Can Island Port, accounted for 68.4% of total non-crude cargo throughput in 2022. This share is consistent with the 2021 figure of 68.1%.

The decline is attributable to the intermittent closure of the Apapa access corridor during road rehabilitation works in the second and third quarters. Despite this, containerised cargo at Apapa increased by 3.2% to 1,021,400 TEU.

Tin Can Island Port handled 5,401,200 metric tonnes of non-crude cargo, an increase of 4.7%. The port benefited from the diversion of services from Apapa during the road works. Containerised cargo at Tin Can Island reached 461,200 TEU, up 6.1% from the previous year.

**Forum Rules and Guidelines – Please Read Before Posting**

*Posted by moderator_team on 15 March 2019, 08:00 WAT – Stickied*

Welcome to the Lagos Port Operations Forum. This forum exists to support the safe, efficient, and transparent exchange of information among port users, terminal operators, agents, pilots, truckers, and other stakeholders. To keep discussions useful and professional, we have adopted the following guidelines. Please read them carefully before posting.

**General Conduct**

- Treat all members with respect. Disagreements about operational matters are welcome, but personal attacks, insults, or abusive language are not permitted.
- Post in English. Nigerian Pidgin is acceptable in casual conversation, but please ensure your message is clear to members who may not be familiar with local slang.
- Do not share confidential commercial information, including cargo manifests, vessel schedules that are not yet public, or terminal pricing agreements.
- Do not post content that is defamatory, discriminatory, or otherwise unlawful under Nigerian law.

**Operational Posts**

- When reporting vessel movements, berth assignments, or equipment status, include the vessel name, IMO number (if known), and the time of the report. This allows other members to verify and cross-reference information.
- If you are reporting a delay or disruption, state the cause and the estimated duration, even if the estimate is rough. A tentative estimate is more useful than no estimate at all.
- Do not post speculative information about accidents, security incidents, or regulatory actions. Wait for official confirmation from the relevant authority (e.g., NPA, Nigerian Customs, terminal management).
- When quoting another member or an external source, use the quote function or clearly attribute the source. Do not present someone else's information as your own.

**Unacceptable Content**

- Spam, including unsolicited advertisements for services unrelated to port operations.
- Requests for unofficial payments or facilitation fees, and any discussion of how to bypass official procedures.
- Political campaigning or religious preaching not related to port operations.
- Multiple duplicate posts or deliberately off-topic messages in operational threads.

**Moderation and Enforcement**

- Moderators may edit or remove posts that violate these guidelines, with or without notice.
- Repeated violations may result in a temporary or permanent ban. Bans are applied by the moderator team and are not subject to negotiation in public threads.
- If you believe a post has been removed in error, contact the moderator team via private message.

**Acknowledgement**

By posting in this forum, you confirm that you have read and understood these guidelines. New members are encouraged to introduce themselves in the Introductions thread before participating in operational discussions.

We thank you for your cooperation and for helping us maintain a valuable resource for the Lagos port community.

---

*Posted by new_member_oyin on 15 March 2019, 09:15 WAT*

Read and understood. I have been posting here for a while and I appreciate the effort to keep things organized. The rule about speculative information is important, especially for safety-related topics.

---

*Posted by danfo_driver_emeka on 15 March 2019, 10:30 WAT*

NIGERIAN PORTS AUTHORITY

PUBLIC NOTICE ON APAPA DREDGING PLAN

The Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) wishes to inform all port users, shipping lines, terminal operators, freight forwarders, and the general public of the planned dredging of the Apapa Port channel and berth pockets. This exercise is part of the Authority’s continuing effort to maintain safe navigational depths and operational efficiency at the Lagos Port Complex.

1. SCOPE OF WORK

The planned dredging will cover the following areas:

(a) The main approach channel from the fairway buoy to the turning basin;

(b) The turning basin itself;

(c) Berth pockets along Apapa Quay, Berths 1 through 10;

(d) The area around the Apapa Bulk Terminal and the Ijora Creek entrance.

The work will involve the removal of accumulated silt and sediment to restore the designed depth of 11.5 metres below chart datum at the berths, and 13.5 metres in the approach channel. Dredged material will be disposed of at the designated offshore spoil grounds in accordance with the approved environmental management plan.

2. PLANNED DATE

The dredging is planned to commence on 2021-03-01. The Authority notes that this date is subject to weather conditions, availability of the dredging plant, and other operational factors. Any change to the planned date will be communicated through a subsequent bulletin.

3. DURATION AND WORKING HOURS

The dredging operation is expected to last approximately twenty-one (21) days, weather permitting. Works will be carried out around the clock, including public holidays, to minimise the overall duration of the exercise. The dredger and attendant tugboats will be displaying the appropriate lights and shapes at night.

4. IMPACT ON PORT OPERATIONS

During the dredging period, there will be temporary disruptions to vessel movements. These include:

(a) One-way traffic in the approach channel at certain stages of the work;

(b) Temporary closure of individual berth pockets as the dredger works along the quay;

(c) Possible delays to vessel berthing and sailing of up to four (4) hours, depending on the stage of the works.

The Authority has put in place a schedule of operations with the Harbour Master’s office to minimise these disruptions. Shipping lines and agents are advised to plan their arrivals accordingly and to liaise with the Port Master’s office for updated berthing windows.

5. SAFETY AND SECURITY

All dredging activities will be conducted in compliance with the International Safety Management (ISM) Code and the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code. The dredger will be attended by security patrol boats at all times. Unauthorised craft are warned to keep clear of the dredging area and its associated floating pipelines.

6. HEALTH, SAFETY, AND ENVIRONMENT

The contractor engaged for this exercise has been directed to comply with all applicable environmental regulations, including the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) guidelines. A pre-dredging environmental baseline survey has been completed, and water quality monitoring will be carried out throughout the operation. Any discharge of dredged material outside the approved spoil grounds is strictly prohibited.

The dredging exercise was undertaken to restore navigable depths at the port's berths, turning basin, and approach channel, which had experienced significant siltation over several years. The works were executed in accordance with the approved design depths and within the spoil grounds designated by the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA).

Key particulars of the completed works are as follows:

- Design depth at berths: 12.0 metres below chart datum
- Design depth at turning basin: 11.5 metres below chart datum
- Design depth at approach channel: 11.0 metres below chart datum
- Total volume of material dredged: approximately 1.2 million cubic metres
- Dredged material disposed at approved offshore spoil grounds

The contractor mobilised a trailing suction hopper dredger and a grab dredger for the exercise. Works commenced on 1 March 2021 and were executed in phases to minimise disruption to port operations. Berths were dredged sequentially, with each berth reopened to traffic immediately upon completion of dredging and post-dredging survey verification.

3. ACHIEVEMENTS

The completion of this dredging plan has restored the port's declared depths, thereby enabling larger vessels to berth safely and improving the overall efficiency of cargo handling operations at Apapa Port. Some of the notable achievements recorded during the exercise include:

- Restoration of full navigable depth at all six (6) berths within the port
- Reduction in vessel waiting time due to tidal restrictions
- Improved safety margins for vessels transiting the approach channel
- Compliance with all environmental monitoring requirements, with no reported incidents of unauthorised discharge

4. POST-DREDGING SURVEY

A post-dredging hydrographic survey was carried out by an independent surveyor between 10 and 14 July 2021. The survey confirmed that all dredged areas met the required design depths. The survey results have been reviewed and accepted by the Authority's Hydrographic Unit, and a copy of the survey report is available for inspection at the Port Manager's office upon written request.

5. SAFETY AND SECURITY

Throughout the dredging exercise, the Authority maintained the highest safety and security standards. The dredgers were attended by security patrol boats at all times, in compliance with the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code. No safety incidents were recorded during the period of the works.

1. POST-DREDGING SURVEY AND CHART UPDATES

Following the completion of the dredging exercise on 15 July 2021, the post-dredging survey was conducted by Messrs. Oceanic Surveys Limited between 20 and 28 July 2021. The survey confirmed that the designed depths were achieved across the full width of the berthing pockets and the turning basin. The survey results have been forwarded to the Nigerian Navy Hydrographic Department for the updating of navigational charts.

Port users are advised that the electronic navigational charts for Apapa Port were updated on 12 August 2021. Mariners should ensure they are using the latest editions of all relevant charts and publications.

2. MAINTENANCE DREDGING – 2022 PROGRAMME

The Authority wishes to inform stakeholders that routine maintenance dredging at Apapa Port has been scheduled for the third quarter of 2022. This exercise will focus on the siltation hotspots identified during the post-dredging survey, particularly at the berth pockets of Berths 1 to 5 and the area adjacent to the container terminal.

The maintenance dredging programme is expected to commence in August 2022 and will last approximately six weeks, subject to weather conditions and equipment availability. The scope of works will include:

- Dredging of berth pockets to the design depth of 10.5 metres below chart datum
- Removal of accumulated silt at the turning basin edges
- Disposal of dredged material at the approved spoil grounds

The Authority will issue a separate notice with detailed information on the maintenance dredging programme, including the name of the contractor and the expected impact on port operations, in due course.

3. APAPA PORT ACCESS ROAD IMPROVEMENT PROJECT

The Authority is working with the Federal Ministry of Works and Housing and the Lagos State Government on the ongoing improvement of the Apapa Port access road network. The project, which commenced in October 2021, involves the reconstruction of the main port access road from the Apapa-Oshodi Expressway to the port gates.

The Authority held a stakeholder engagement forum on 16 December 2021 at the Lagos Port Complex Conference Room. The forum was attended by representatives of shipping lines, terminal operators, freight forwarders, customs brokers, and other port users.

compilation as maintained by the Statistics Branch. The Eastgate figure of 450,000 TEU
is current as of the date of this report and reflects the terminal's full-year
operational output; no revision has been issued.

6.3 Terminal-Level Commentary

APM Terminals Apapa remains the single largest container terminal in the country,
handling 32.4% of total container throughput. The terminal operated at an average
berth productivity of 28 moves per crane-hour during the year, a marginal improvement
over the 2021 figure of 27 moves per crane-hour.

Tin Can Island Container Terminal recorded the second-highest throughput. The terminal
benefited from the diversion of some services from Apapa during the periods when the
Lagos Port Complex access road was under repair. Its average crane productivity was 24
moves per crane-hour, with a peak of 31 moves recorded in October.

Eastgate recorded a throughput of 450,000 TEU in 2022, a 7.3% increase over the
previous year. The terminal's growth was driven by the addition of two new ship-to-shore
gantry cranes in the first quarter and the expansion of its empty container storage yard,
which added 4,500 ground slots. Eastgate also reported an average truck turnaround time
of 48 minutes, which is among the best in the Western Ports complex. The terminal's
current controlled entry for 2022 is as stated above, with no pending revision.

Port & Cargo Handling Services recorded a decline of 2.6%. The decline is attributed to
the loss of one major shipping line service, which relocated to Eastgate in March 2022.
The terminal's management has indicated that it expects to recover the lost volume in
2023 through a new service agreement signed in December.

Five Star Logistics recorded the highest growth rate among the Tin Can Island terminals
at 12.4%. This growth is attributable to increased RoRo-related container movements,
as the terminal serves as a transhipment point for vehicles imported through the
neighbouring RoRo berth.

West Africa Container Terminal at Onne Port recorded the highest growth rate overall at
15.2%, albeit from a small base. The terminal is the sole container facility in the
Eastern Ports and continues to benefit from the expansion of manufacturing activity in
the Onne Oil and Gas Free Zone.

4.1 Western Ports (Lagos) Commodity Detail

The Western Ports, comprising the Lagos Port Complex (Apapa) and Tin Can Island Port, accounted for 68.4% of total non-crude cargo throughput in 2022. This share is consistent with the 2021 figure of 68.1%.

Apapa Port handled 4,862,300 metric tonnes of non-crude cargo, a decrease of 1.8% compared with 2021. The decline is attributable to the intermittent closure of the Apapa access corridor during road rehabilitation works in the second and third quarters. Despite this, containerised cargo at Apapa increased by 3.2% to 1,021,400 TEU.

Tin Can Island Port handled 5,401,200 metric tonnes of non-crude cargo, an increase of 4.7%. The port benefited from the diversion of services from Apapa during the road works. Containerised cargo at Tin Can Island reached 461,200 TEU, up 6.1% from the previous year.

4.1.2 Terminal Notes

Apapa Container Terminal (ACT) remains the single largest container terminal in the country, handling 532,100 TEU in 2022. This represents 32.4% of total national container throughput. The terminal operated at an average berth productivity of 28 moves per crane-hour during the year, a marginal improvement over the 2021 figure of 27 moves per crane-hour. The terminal also commissioned two additional rubber-tyred gantry cranes in November, which are expected to improve yard operations in 2023.
